questions.q: How does the article describe political authority?
options: A burden best refused
Not quite. The article says: A test entrusted for a limited time – what matters is how it is used, not how long it is held.
A reward for good character
Not quite. The article says: A test entrusted for a limited time – what matters is how it is used, not how long it is held.
A test entrusted for a limited time – what matters is how it is used, not how long it is held
Yes. “Such days We alternate among the people.”
A permanent possession of those who win it
Not quite. The article says: A test entrusted for a limited time – what matters is how it is used, not how long it is held.
questions.rationale: “Political authority is not a prize to be permanently owned. Rather, it is a test entrusted to human beings for a limited period.”

questions.q: What does understanding the temporary nature of power help people avoid?
options: Excessive pride in success and excessive despair in setbacks
Right. It gives inner stability and the ability to adjust.
All interest in public life
Not quite. The article says: Excessive pride in success and excessive despair in setbacks.
The need to work
Not quite. The article says: Excessive pride in success and excessive despair in setbacks.
Contact with other communities
Not quite. The article says: Excessive pride in success and excessive despair in setbacks.
questions.rationale: “Recognizing this reality helps people avoid excessive pride during success and excessive despair during setbacks.”

questions.q: Why did a home-grown tomato fill the writer with awe when a market tomato does not?
options: Tomatoes are rare
Not quite. The article says: Watching it grow lifted “the veil of habit,” showing a process no human can create.
It had cost a great deal to grow
Not quite. The article says: Watching it grow lifted “the veil of habit,” showing a process no human can create.
Watching it grow lifted “the veil of habit,” showing a process no human can create
Yes. “Then let man look at his food.”
It was larger than market tomatoes
Not quite. The article says: Watching it grow lifted “the veil of habit,” showing a process no human can create.
questions.rationale: “When we personally observe the process of growth, the veil of habit is lifted. We begin to see creation with fresh eyes.”

questions.q: Seeing a leafless tree covered in red flowers, what did Maulana Wahiduddin Khan pray?
options: That the tree might bear fruit
Not quite. The article says: That God, who brings flowers from a barren tree, might bring spiritual growth into his own “barren being”.
That God, who brings flowers from a barren tree, might bring spiritual growth into his own “barren being”
Well read. Dryness is not always the final reality.
That the journey might end soon
Not quite. The article says: That God, who brings flowers from a barren tree, might bring spiritual growth into his own “barren being”.
That he might own such a tree
Not quite. The article says: That God, who brings flowers from a barren tree, might bring spiritual growth into his own “barren being”.
questions.rationale: “O God, I too am a barren existence. As You can bring such beautiful flowers out of a dry and barren tree, bring spiritual growth and realization into my barren being.”

questions.q: What does the article call the real danger in life?
options: Being criticised
Not quite. The article says: Losing hope – not failure, criticism or rejection.
Having too little money
Not quite. The article says: Losing hope – not failure, criticism or rejection.
Losing hope – not failure, criticism or rejection
Correct. Hardships are meant to awaken and strengthen.
Failing at a task
Not quite. The article says: Losing hope – not failure, criticism or rejection.
questions.rationale: “The real danger in life is therefore not failure, criticism, or rejection. The real danger is losing hope.”

questions.q: What does the article mean when it says many people “stop at the signpost”?
options: They travel without a map
Not quite. The article says: They enjoy the blessing but go no further to recognise the Giver behind it.
They enjoy the blessing but go no further to recognise the Giver behind it
Yes. They miss the greater joy of realization.
They refuse to enjoy anything
Not quite. The article says: They enjoy the blessing but go no further to recognise the Giver behind it.
They read signs too slowly
Not quite. The article says: They enjoy the blessing but go no further to recognise the Giver behind it.
questions.rationale: “Every enjoyment in life is a signpost pointing toward its Creator. Unfortunately, many people stop at the signpost and never continue the journey.”

questions.q: Looking back on fifty years of travel, what does the writer say about the hostility people often expect from others?
options: It depends entirely on one’s clothes
Not quite. The article says: Much of it exists in the mind more than in the world; approaching people with trust and goodwill usually brings the same in return.
It is always worse than expected
Not quite. The article says: Much of it exists in the mind more than in the world; approaching people with trust and goodwill usually brings the same in return.
It can be avoided only by staying at home
Not quite. The article says: Much of it exists in the mind more than in the world; approaching people with trust and goodwill usually brings the same in return.
Much of it exists in the mind more than in the world; approaching people with trust and goodwill usually brings the same in return
Right. “Avoid much suspicion.”
questions.rationale: “Very often, the fears that dominate our minds do not exist in the external world to the extent that we imagine.”

questions.q: In a storm small birds struggle at the same level, while large birds do something different. What, and what is the lesson?
options: They fly into it – one should confront every challenge
Not quite. The article says: They rise above it – a wise person rises above reaction and is not ruled by every unpleasant remark.
They hide – one should avoid all difficulty
Not quite. The article says: They rise above it – a wise person rises above reaction and is not ruled by every unpleasant remark.
They rise above it – a wise person rises above reaction and is not ruled by every unpleasant remark
Yes. Patience is strength.
They land – one should give up
Not quite. The article says: They rise above it – a wise person rises above reaction and is not ruled by every unpleasant remark.
questions.rationale: “Large birds… use their powerful wings to rise above it… A wise person adopts a different approach. He rises above the level of reaction.”

questions.q: Asked why he kept speaking when people did not change, Krishnamurti replied, “Have you ever asked a rose why it blooms?” What is the point?
options: Speaking is useless
Not quite. The article says: Goodness should flow from one’s nature, not depend on others’ appreciation or response.
Goodness should flow from one’s nature, not depend on others’ appreciation or response
Exactly. Motivation comes from within.
Audiences should be chosen carefully
Not quite. The article says: Goodness should flow from one’s nature, not depend on others’ appreciation or response.
Roses bloom only when admired
Not quite. The article says: Goodness should flow from one’s nature, not depend on others’ appreciation or response.
questions.rationale: “A person of wisdom does not make goodness dependent on people’s responses… His motivation comes from within, not from public approval.”

questions.q: A mother asked who would inherit her wealthy son’s riches. What deeper question does the article put in its place?
options: Who will manage his business?
Not quite. The article says: What will the man himself take with him after death?.
How can the wealth be divided fairly?
Not quite. The article says: What will the man himself take with him after death?.
What will the man himself take with him after death?
Well reasoned. Only inner wealth – faith, sincerity, good deeds – goes with him.
How much tax will be due?
Not quite. The article says: What will the man himself take with him after death?.
questions.rationale: “Instead of asking who would inherit the man’s wealth, one should ask: What will the man himself take with him after death?”
